title: The Chronicle of ʿAlī ibn Turka

verdict.manText: He lost the third inquisition with nothing left to spend — no patron, no standing, and a file thick enough to bury anyone.
verdict.systemText: The astrological-lettrist platform becomes the default imperial cosmology — Timurid, Aqquyunlu, Safavid, Uzbek, Ottoman, Mughal. Courts he never saw will run on his mathematics for centuries.

legacyNotes: He taught widely and hoarded jealously by turns — reach for the doctrine, reserve for its operative core — and the tension was never resolved, only lived.
He wore Akhlātī’s name openly, and it preceded him everywhere afterward.
He was there the night the circle took the Brethren’s name.
Qāsim-i Anvār counted him a brother, and that ledger stayed open for life.
The madrasa credential was real, and it was worth exactly what it cost him at the tribunals.
He was of Akhlātī’s circle, whatever he later said about it.
He was, on the record, a judge who ruled against powerful men — which made his name and his enemies together.
He freed an accused man on procedure and let the room believe he knew nothing of the science.
His kin died believing the Cairo years had been an ordinary education.
A warrāq in Isfahan was the first person besides himself to write his words out.
He arrived at court as what he was, apparatus and all.
He was Iskandar Sultan’s man in the years when that was the most interesting and most dangerous thing to be.
He promised a prince a spectacle, in writing, with a season named for it.
He missed a patron’s deadline. Courts remember misses far longer than successes.
He told a prince the cosmos had written his house into it — the most useful and most quotable thing he ever said.
A court calligrapher became his collaborator, and made his science visible.
An atelier made his cosmogram in gold, and other courts asked for copies.
When the court broke up he left with his papers and no allegiances.
He attempted the whole architecture at once — the first summa of its kind ever tried.
He explained his diagrams and translated his terms for every audience — against the whole habit of the tradition.
He met the first summons with a defense prepared in full.
He won the first inquisition.
He won the second inquisition too. Two acquittals is not the same thing as safety.
At the third tribunal he refused to bend — the one thing about him the record is certain of.
He taught in every town that let him stop, and the teaching did not end when he did.
The bench went unserved while he wrote, and the city noticed which he had chosen.
The Investigations exists. Whatever else is true, he wrote the book.
The summa stands in dense Arabic — a masterwork for the few who could climb it.
He held judicial standing to the end, in name if not always in fact.
He was, first and last, a judge of Isfahan.
He bought his books through the eastern gate with the money his exile was to live on.

attested.hist: He studied in Cairo under Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī, lettrist, alchemist and geomancer.
He served as Chief Judge of Isfahan, famous for defending the weak against the powerful.
attested.yours: you took the bench and ruled as he did.

attested.hist: In 1420 he completed Investigations — the first systematic summa of Islamic lettrism — as Ulugh Beg broke ground on the Samarkand observatory.
His central diagram, the Ṭahawī Circle, survives in his own handwriting (Tehran, Majlis Library MS 10196, f. 63a).
attested.yours: you never drew the Circle; your system has no surviving image.

attested.hist: He faced three state inquisitions engineered by rival colleagues: he won the first two and lost the third, c. 1427.
attested.yours: the same road, ending the same way.

attested.hist: Qāsim-i Anvār, his Cairo companion, was exiled in 1427 over the same lettrist associations.
attested.yours: in your life the friendship never came to its test.

attested.hist: He died in 1432, impoverished and in legal limbo, after five years of wandering exile; Yazdī — who copied his autograph — outlived him by twenty-two years, and the platform they built became imperial cosmology across six court cultures.
attested.yours: your Yazdī never copied the work — history’s own transmission route, closed.

log.rubric: AT THE MADRASA · MORNING LESSONS
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Formation (Cairo); VN c01
log.situation: The law professors teach what Cairo certifies: jurisprudence, disputation, the instruments of a judge’s career. It is slow, orthodox, and respected — and it is the credential your family’s judicial line expects of you.

options.label: Commit to rigorous scholastic training
options.detail: The long path: law, logic, credentials no inquisitor can question.

options.label: Attend only enough to pass unremarked
options.detail: Keep the seat warm; spend your real hours elsewhere in the city.

log.outcomeText: The professors mark you as serious. The credential begins to exist.

chronicle.orig: In Cairo he sat before the jurists and learned the law’s long patience.
chronicle.current: In Cairo he sat before the jurists and learned the law’s long patience.

log.rubric: AT THE MADRASA · A PUBLIC DISPUTATION
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Formation; disputation was the standard exam form
log.situation: A visiting jurist stakes a position on the limits of permissible sciences, and the hall turns to the students. A strong answer is a reputation. A clever one is a risk. Silence is also an answer.

options.label: Argue squarely within the law
options.detail: Win as a jurist. Say nothing the hall can quote against you later.

options.label: Defend the mathematical sciences by demonstration
options.detail: Show the hall that number underlies the very logic they argue with.

options.label: Hold your tongue
options.detail: A student’s silence costs nothing today. Perhaps something later.

log.outcomeText: A solid showing. The professors nod; nothing is risked.

chronicle.orig: He held his own in disputation and gave the hall nothing to whisper about.
chronicle.current: He held his own in disputation and gave the hall nothing to whisper about.

log.rubric: A COURTYARD OFF THE COPPERSMITHS’ STREET · AFTER DARK
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Formation (Cairo): studied under Akhlāṭī
log.situation: Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī receives students the madrasa would never admit to envying. On his table: letter-tables, a geomancer’s brass instrument, a crucible still warm. He asks one question — what do you want to learn first?

plate.caption: Geomantic instrument, Egypt or Syria, 1241/42 CE — British Museum (via Wikimedia Commons)

options.label: The science of letters
options.detail: Līmiyā: talismans, letter-grids, the mathematics hiding inside the alphabet.

options.label: The work of the furnace
options.detail: Kīmiyā: substances, operations, the elite and expensive art.

options.label: The figures in the sand
options.detail: Geomancy — Akhlāṭī’s own third art, quick to learn, easy to sneer at, oddly reliable.

log.outcomeText: He sets a letter-grid before you and begins with the value of the alif. The door is open.

chronicle.orig: He came to Akhlāṭī’s courtyard and began with the letters, as the tradition begins.
chronicle.current: He came to Akhlāṭī’s courtyard and began with the letters, as the tradition begins.

log.rubric: AKHLĀṬĪ’S COURTYARD · THE MASTER’S REQUEST
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Formation; the publicness of the tie is undocumented (VN c02)
log.situation: Akhlāṭī’s name travels — admired in three languages, denounced in two. Tonight he asks, mildly, whether you will let it be known whose student you are. The question is a door with two hinges: honor, and exposure.

options.label: Declare the discipleship openly
options.detail: Wear his name. His enemies become yours; so do his friends.

options.label: Study on, but privately
options.detail: Keep the learning; skip the label. He will understand. Probably.

log.outcomeText: Word moves through the quarter in a week. Doors open that you did not know existed — and one or two close.

chronicle.orig: He let Cairo know whose student he was, and accepted everything the name carried.
chronicle.current: He let Cairo know whose student he was, and accepted everything the name carried.

log.rubric: AKHLĀṬĪ’S COURTYARD · AN ARGUMENT OF FATHERS
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Formation: first to pair Ibn ʿArabī and Ḥamūya as co-founders (VN c05)
log.situation: The circle quarrels amiably over descent: is the science of letters Ibn ʿArabī’s, the Andalusian Supreme Master’s — or Saʿd al-Dīn Ḥamūya’s, his Iranian twin? Partisans of each want you. Akhlāṭī watches to see how you think.

plate.caption: Magic squares (awfāq) and letter-grid tables — Shams al-Maʿārif, printed edition (Wikimedia Commons)

options.label: Stand with Ibn ʿArabī’s line
options.detail: The prestigious answer — the West’s Supreme Master, safest to cite.

options.label: Stand with Ḥamūya’s line
options.detail: The Iranian answer — obscurer, stranger, closer to home.

options.label: Insist the two are co-founders
options.detail: The synthesis no one else will make. Pleases neither faction — yet.

log.outcomeText: A defensible flag. The Ḥamūya men shrug and let it pass.

chronicle.orig: Pressed on the lineage of letters, he named Ibn ʿArabī and stood with the many.
chronicle.current: Pressed on the lineage of letters, he named Ibn ʿArabī and stood with the many.

log.rubric: AKHLĀṬĪ’S COURTYARD · THE CIRCLE TAKES A NAME
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Formation: the circle’s self-naming as Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ
log.situation: Late, lamps low, someone says it aloud: this circle should call itself Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ — the Brethren of Purity, the name of the old encyclopedists of Basra. To take a four-hundred-year-old banner is not a joke. Everyone looks at everyone.

options.label: Take the name, and say why
options.detail: Argue the old Brethren’s project unfinished — and this circle its heirs.

options.label: Warn against a name that can be indicted
options.detail: A named circle is a thing a court can point at. Stay a rumor.

log.outcomeText: The name is taken half in earnest, half in delight. Names taken in delight have a way of becoming earnest.

chronicle.orig: The circle called itself the New Brethren of Purity, half a jest that everyone knew was not one.
chronicle.current: The circle called itself the New Brethren of Purity, half a jest that everyone knew was not one.

log.rubric: AT THE KHĀNQĀH · A POET IN FULL FLIGHT
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Formation: Qāsim-i Anvār a close Cairo companion (VN c04)
log.situation: Qāsim-i Anvār recites and the whole khānqāh forgets to breathe. Afterward he finds you, laughing, quoting your own question back at you improved. Men like this either become your brother or your epitaph. Sometimes both.

options.label: Let the friendship go deep
options.detail: Brotherhood with the most magnetic — and least careful — man in Cairo.

options.label: Keep a warm distance
options.detail: Enjoy the verses; skip the entanglement. Poets attract weather.

log.outcomeText: The friendship takes — and with it, the first raised eyebrow from the sober men of the lodge.

chronicle.orig: He walked openly with Qāsim-i Anvār, and the careful men began to keep a small ledger of it.
chronicle.current: He walked openly with Qāsim-i Anvār, and the careful men began to keep a small ledger of it.

log.rubric: THE ROAD HOME · CAIRO ENDS
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Formation: Akhlāṭī dies 1397; the return to Iran follows
log.situation: Word runs through the quarter like cold water: Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī is dead. The circle stands in his courtyard not knowing where to put its hands. Cairo is finished for you — the question is only what you carry to Isfahan, and how.

plate.caption: Teardrop cosmological diagram — Shams al-Maʿārif, p. 256 (Wikimedia Commons)

options.label: Leave as his acknowledged student
options.detail: Claim the inheritance aloud. The name will reach Isfahan before you do.

options.label: Carry the Brethren’s letters east
options.detail: Leave as the network’s courier: introductions from Cairo to all Iran.

options.label: Return as a jurist, nothing more
options.detail: Fold the Cairo years away. Arrive in Isfahan clean, credentialed, unremarked.

options.label: Travel in company with Yazdī
options.detail: Share the road with your brother in God. The system’s first two carriers, together.

log.outcomeText: You speak at the gathering as one of his own. Men you have never met will now write to you for years.

chronicle.orig: When Akhlāṭī died, he stood forth as the master’s student, and let the inheritance be seen.
chronicle.current: When Akhlāṭī died, he stood forth as the master’s student, and let the inheritance be seen.

log.rubric: THE TRIBUNAL · THE OFFICE OFFERED
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Vitals: Chief Judge (qāḍī) of Isfahan
log.situation: The bench your father sat on is open, and the city expects a Turka on it. The office pays, protects, and confers the one credential no accusation slides off easily: you would be a judge, not merely a man with opinions.

options.label: Take the judgeship
options.detail: Salary, standing, and a permanent claim on your hours.

options.label: Refuse the bench
options.detail: Keep every hour for the work. Lose the shield the office would have been.

options.label: Serve, but seek a deputy first
options.detail: Take the office and immediately find someone to carry half of it.

log.outcomeText: You are invested as qāḍī of Isfahan. The docket is already full.

chronicle.orig: He took his father’s bench and became a judge of Isfahan.
chronicle.current: He took his father’s bench and became a judge of Isfahan.

log.rubric: THE TRIBUNAL · A POWERFUL MAN AND A POOR ONE
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — known specifically as a judge who defended the weak against the powerful
log.situation: A landowner with friends at the governor’s house has taken a smallholder’s water rights. The law is not ambiguous. The landowner’s expectation that this will not matter is also not ambiguous.

options.label: Rule for the smallholder
options.detail: The law as written. It will cost you a friend you do not have yet.

options.label: Force a settlement instead
options.detail: Both sides walk away irritated and intact. No enemy, no precedent.

options.label: Rule for the landowner and bank the favor
options.detail: A powerful house owes you. That is a real asset, honestly obtained by dishonest means.

log.outcomeText: You rule correctly and quietly. Justice done; enemy acquired at a discount.

chronicle.orig: He ruled against the powerful man, and the powerful man remembered it.
chronicle.current: He ruled against the powerful man, and the powerful man remembered it.

log.rubric: THE TRIBUNAL · AN ACCUSATION OF SORCERY
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — occult jurisprudence; the specific case is constructed
log.situation: A man is charged with sorcery. On the evidence table: sand-boards, a chart of figures, a client list. You are the one judge in Isfahan who can tell at a glance that this is geomancy — a technical craft, badly practiced. Saying so out loud tells the room how you know.

plate.caption: Arabic diagram of geomantic figures classification, 15th c. (Wikimedia Commons)

options.label: Acquit on the technical ground
options.detail: Explain what the evidence actually is. Everyone learns you can read it.

options.label: Acquit on procedure — say nothing about the craft
options.detail: The witnesses are inadequate. That is enough, and it reveals nothing.

options.label: Convict him
options.detail: Distance yourself decisively. It is a defensible verdict and an ugly one.

log.outcomeText: Insufficient testimony; case dismissed. The man goes home, the room learns nothing, and you sleep well enough.

chronicle.orig: He freed the accused on the testimony, and let the court believe he knew nothing of the art.
chronicle.current: He freed the accused on the testimony, and let the court believe he knew nothing of the art.

log.rubric: THE FAMILY HOUSE · WHAT THE HOUSE EXPECTS
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — the Turka family judicial line; the domestic scene is constructed
log.situation: Your kin want to know what Cairo was for. There is a family library of law and hadith, a family reputation, and a family assumption that the strange years abroad are now concluded.

options.label: Tell them what they want to hear
options.detail: Cairo was training. Nothing more. The house relaxes.

options.label: Tell them the truth and ask for the library
options.detail: Make the family an asset instead of an audience. Risky; they vote.

log.outcomeText: The house is satisfied and the doors of Isfahan’s respectable society stay open.

chronicle.orig: He let his family believe the Cairo years had been an ordinary education.
chronicle.current: He let his family believe the Cairo years had been an ordinary education.

log.rubric: THE WARRĀQ’S SHOP · A MAN WHO COPIES ANYTHING
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — manuscript culture; this copyist is constructed
log.situation: The warrāq works fast, charges fairly, and has never once asked what a text is for. Everything you have written so far exists in exactly one copy, in your own hand, in a house that could burn.

options.label: Commission copies of your notes
options.detail: Transmission begins with a second copy existing at all.

options.label: Copy everything in your own hand
options.detail: Slower, safer, and no stranger has read a line of it.

log.outcomeText: Two clean copies inside a month. One stays with you; one goes into a chest at your uncle’s.

chronicle.orig: He put his notes into a copyist’s hands, and his work existed in more than one place for the first time.
chronicle.current: He put his notes into a copyist’s hands, and his work existed in more than one place for the first time.

log.rubric: THE SUMMONS · A PRINCE SENDS FOR YOU
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — attachment to Iskandar Sultan’s court c. 1409
log.situation: A courier in Timurid livery, a sealed letter, and an invitation that is not really one: Iskandar Sultan, prince and governor of Fars, has heard there is a judge in Isfahan who reads more than law. The Isfahan years end here.

options.label: Go, and bring the whole apparatus
options.detail: Books, tables, instruments, ambitions. Arrive as what you actually are.

options.label: Go as a jurist, and let them discover the rest
options.detail: Arrive credentialed and unremarkable. Reveal the work when the room is right.

options.label: Go, and bring your people
options.detail: A copyist, a correspondent, a friend. Arrive as a circle, not a man.

log.outcomeText: You ride south with three chests of paper and no intention of being anyone’s ornament.

chronicle.orig: He went to Iskandar Sultan’s court openly, bringing his whole apparatus with him.
chronicle.current: He went to Iskandar Sultan’s court openly, bringing his whole apparatus with him.

log.rubric: THE AUDIENCE HALL · WHOSE MAN WILL YOU BE
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Iskandar Sultan (c.1409–1415), then Bāysunghur (from c.1416)
log.situation: Two houses want you, and a third possibility exists. Iskandar Sultan’s court at Shiraz fuses star science, poetry and painting — brilliant and politically exposed. Bāysunghur, Shāh Rukh’s son, offers the finest book-workshop in the world and a father who is currently winning. Samarkand offers mathematics and Ulugh Beg.

options.label: Take service with Iskandar Sultan
options.detail: The experimental court: everything permitted, nothing guaranteed.

options.label: Take service with Bāysunghur
options.detail: The manuscript machine, and the safer branch of the dynasty.

options.label: Go to Samarkand with Yazdī
options.detail: Mathematics, instruments, and the observatory rising. Requires your brother in God.

log.outcomeText: Iskandar receives you like a discovery. His workshop already contains an astrologer, two poets and a painter arguing about the same diagram.

chronicle.orig: He entered the service of Iskandar Sultan, in whose workshop star science and painting shared a table.
chronicle.current: He entered the service of Iskandar Sultan, in whose workshop star science and painting shared a table.

log.rubric: THE AUDIENCE HALL · THE PATRON WANTS SOMETHING USEFUL
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — works commissioned as royal "boons"; patronage was transactional and explicit
log.situation: The commission is put plainly, which is how commissions are put: something demonstrable, by a named season, in exchange for money and standing. The prince does not want a philosophy. He wants a result he can show people.

options.label: Promise a public demonstration
options.detail: The big claim. Big reward if you land it — and a promise a court can measure.

options.label: Promise a written exposition instead
options.detail: Smaller claim, likelier delivery. Patrons remember who does not miss.

options.label: Negotiate the terms down
options.detail: Longer deadline, smaller reward. The professional’s answer.

options.label: Decline the commission
options.detail: Take no money and make no promise. Costs standing; costs nothing else.

log.outcomeText: Agreed, witnessed, and written into the household accounts. You have four seasons and a promise with your name on it.

chronicle.orig: He promised the prince a public demonstration of his science, with a season named for it.
chronicle.current: He promised the prince a public demonstration of his science, with a season named for it.

log.rubric: THE AUDIENCE HALL · THE PRINCE’S QUESTION
log.source: BIOGRAPHY / RESEARCH — lettrism as imperial political theory ("the political was and is magical as a rule")
log.situation: He has been thinking, which is dangerous in princes. "If the letters are the architecture of creation," he says, "what does that tell us about the architecture of kingship?" The hall goes quiet. This is the question your whole science exists to answer, asked by a man who can act on the answer.

options.label: Answer: it makes kingship a discipline he must study
options.detail: Turn the flattery into an obligation. Philosopher-kingship, argued to his face.

options.label: Answer: it shows his house was written into the cosmos
options.detail: Give him the legitimation he is fishing for. Enormously useful; hard to take back.

options.label: Refuse to reduce the science to statecraft
options.detail: Tell a prince, politely, that the answer is not for him. Nobody does this.

log.outcomeText: It lands beautifully and travels badly. By spring, rivals are quoting it as proof your science is politics in a robe.

chronicle.orig: His legitimating answer was repeated everywhere, most often by men using it against him.
chronicle.current: His legitimating answer was repeated everywhere, most often by men using it against him.

log.rubric: THE KITĀBKHĀNA · THE CALLIGRAPHER HAS FOUND A PATTERN
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Bāysunghur’s atelier and calligraphic culture; this calligrapher is constructed
log.situation: The court calligrapher has been laying out a square Kufic panel and has noticed that the letters, forced into a grid, generate the same proportions in three different verses. She wants to know whether she has found something or merely made something. It is, exactly, your question.

plate.caption: Square Kufic Bismillah page by Ahmed Karahisari, 16th c. (Wikimedia Commons)

options.label: Work it out with her
options.detail: Take an artisan seriously as a colleague. Gains a capability, not a compliment.

options.label: Take the observation and thank her
options.detail: It is a real finding. It can be yours. She is an artisan; nobody will ask.

options.label: Tell her it is an artifact of the grid
options.detail: Probably true. Definitely discouraging. Costs you nothing and closes a door.

log.outcomeText: Half discovery, half artifact of the grid — but the collaboration is real and she will bring you the next one too.

chronicle.orig: He took the calligrapher’s pattern seriously, and she brought him every pattern she found thereafter.
chronicle.current: He took the calligrapher’s pattern seriously, and she brought him every pattern she found thereafter.

log.rubric: THE KITĀBKHĀNA · YOUR DIAGRAM, PROPERLY MADE
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Bāysunghur as accomplished calligrapher and patron of the book arts
log.situation: The kitābkhāna offers to make one of your cosmological diagrams the way it makes things for princes: gold, lapis, a full folio. A diagram that beautiful is an argument that travels — and a diagram that beautiful is also evidence.

plate.caption: Safavid illuminated manuscript page, Shahnameh tradition (Wikimedia Commons)

options.label: Let them make it magnificent
options.detail: Gold and lapis. The system becomes an object princes want to own.

options.label: Insist on a plain, teachable version
options.detail: Simple, explained, reproducible by any copyist. Designed for uptake, not for princes.

options.label: Keep the diagram out of the workshop
options.detail: No copies, no folio, no evidence. The cleanest way to stay small.

log.outcomeText: The finished folio stops conversation. Two other courts request copies within the year — your cosmology is now a luxury good, and luxury goods travel.

chronicle.orig: The atelier made his cosmogram in gold and lapis, and other courts began asking for copies.
chronicle.current: The atelier made his cosmogram in gold and lapis, and other courts began asking for copies.

log.rubric: TOWARD 1420 · THE COURT YEARS END
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — Iskandar Sultan defeated, blinded and executed 1415; patronage shifts to Bāysunghur c.1416
log.situation: Courts end. Iskandar Sultan overreached his uncle Shāh Rukh and paid for it in the way Timurid princes do; the workshops disperse, the patronage reshuffles, and men who were somebody last spring are looking for a house. What you take out of these years is the material the summa will be built from.

plate.caption: "Caesar Makes a Talisman", folio from a Shahnama, Iran c. 1330–40 — MET (CC0)

options.label: Leave with the work, and nothing else
options.detail: Books, tables, diagrams. Let the politics go on without you.

options.label: Attach yourself to the surviving house
options.detail: Bāysunghur’s establishment endures. Continuity of protection, at the price of visible loyalty.

options.label: Leave with your people
options.detail: Calligrapher, astronomer, student, friend — whoever will come. The circle over the career.

log.outcomeText: You go with chests of paper and no faction. It is the least dangerous way to leave a court that has just eaten a prince.

chronicle.orig: When the court broke up he left with his papers and no allegiances.
chronicle.current: When the court broke up he left with his papers and no allegiances.

log.rubric: THE DESK · BEGINNING THE SUMMA
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — 1420: completes Investigations (Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ), the first systematic summa of Islamic lettrism
log.situation: Twenty years of notes, and the shape of the thing is finally visible: not a commentary, not a manual, but a systematic philosophy in which letter, number, and cosmos are one science. It has never been done. The only question is what kind of book it will be.

options.label: Build it as a complete philosophical system
options.detail: The whole architecture, argued from first principles. Slow, enormous, and unprecedented.

options.label: Build it as a usable handbook
options.detail: Method first, philosophy implicit. Less glory, far more uptake.

options.label: Not yet — spend the year deepening instead
options.detail: Refuse to publish prematurely. The system gets better; the years do not come back.

log.outcomeText: The architecture holds on paper. Whether it holds for a reader is a different question, and one you will not be able to ask yourself.

chronicle.orig: He set out to build the whole system at once, and did not stop to ask whether it could be read.
chronicle.current: He set out to build the whole system at once, and did not stop to ask whether it could be read.

log.rubric: THE DESK · IN WHICH LANGUAGE, AND FOR WHOM
log.source: BIOGRAPHY / RESEARCH — dense elite Arabic vs. accessible Persian exposition; de-esotericization as a live strategic axis
log.situation: Arabic is the language of the learned world and of every authority you cite. Persian is the language princes, poets and administrators actually read for pleasure. The same argument in the two languages is not the same argument: one is a monument, the other is an infection.

options.label: Dense Arabic, for the qualified few
options.detail: A masterwork that only the equipped can climb. Prestige, precision, control.

options.label: Persian, for warlords and administrators
options.detail: Reach. Turn princes into philosophers by making the philosophy readable.

options.label: Both: the summa in Arabic, a Persian exposition beside it
options.detail: Two books, two audiences, twice the work. The historically Turkian answer.

log.outcomeText: The prose is magnificent and nearly impassable. Precisely the readers you want will get through it. Precisely no one else will.

chronicle.orig: He wrote the summa in Arabic dense enough to keep out everyone he had not written it for.
chronicle.current: He wrote the summa in Arabic dense enough to keep out everyone he had not written it for.

log.rubric: THE DESK · WHAT TO CONCEAL AND WHAT TO EXPLAIN
log.source: RESEARCH — Investigations’ diagrams deliberately simple and explained, terminology adapted for reception across scholarly communities
log.situation: Every esoteric tradition you inherited hides its operative core behind allusion. You could do that. Or you could explain the diagrams, define the terms, and adapt the vocabulary so that a philosopher, a jurist and a mathematician each find a handhold. The tradition would call the second choice a betrayal.

options.label: Explain everything, and adapt the terminology
options.detail: Design the book for uptake. Diagrams simple; terms translated per audience.

options.label: Explain the frame, conceal the operative core
options.detail: The classic compromise: teachable philosophy, guarded practice.

options.label: Write it for those who already know
options.detail: Allusion, compression, no concessions. The tradition’s own way.

log.outcomeText: You write the same doctrine in four vocabularies and label the diagrams like a teacher. It is the least mysterious esoteric book ever written, and it will therefore actually spread.

chronicle.orig: He explained his diagrams and translated his terms for every audience, against the whole habit of the tradition.
chronicle.current: He explained his diagrams and translated his terms for every audience, against the whole habit of the tradition.

log.rubric: THE FIRST SUMMONS · A TRIBUNAL SENDS FOR YOU
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — three state inquisitions, engineered by jealous rival colleagues, from the 1420s
log.situation: It arrives with a seal and a date: you are required to answer questions concerning your doctrine. It is not, yet, a trial. It has been engineered by colleagues — men who know exactly what to quote, because you wrote it down and let it circulate. The rest of your life begins with this letter.

options.label: Go, and prepare a full defense
options.detail: Answer the summons on its own terms, with everything you have.

options.label: Go, but send to your patron first
options.detail: Spend political protection before spending arguments.

options.label: Go quietly, and concede whatever is cheap
options.detail: Give them small things early. Survive the first one; think about the rest later.

log.outcomeText: You spend the last free season assembling authorities, precedents, and creeds. Whatever else happens, they will have to argue with you.

chronicle.orig: He answered the first summons with a defense prepared in full.
chronicle.current: He answered the first summons with a defense prepared in full.

log.rubric: THE TRIBUNAL · THE FIRST INQUISITION
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — three state inquisitions engineered by rival colleagues; he wins the first two
log.situation: The charge is framed around Qurʾan 2:102 and the angels at Babel who taught men magic: whatever you call your ʿilm al-ḥurūf, the prosecution says, this is what it descends from. Your accusers are colleagues. They have read you closely, which is the problem.

plate.caption: The fallen angels Hārūt and Mārūt, suspended at Babel — Iran, 16th–17th c. (Wikimedia Commons)

options.label: Distinguish theoretical lettrism from sorcery
options.detail: The core legal argument: a mathematics of letters is not an operation on spirits.

options.label: Answer with a creedal statement
options.detail: Give them orthodoxy in your own words — the apology as a genre.

options.label: Attack the accusers’ standing
options.detail: Name the jealousy. Aggressive, satisfying, and it escalates.

log.outcomeText: You hold the distinction for three hours and the panel accepts it. Acquitted — and every word of your defense is now a public document your enemies can study.

chronicle.orig: At the first tribunal he separated the science of letters from sorcery, and was acquitted.
chronicle.current: At the first tribunal he separated the science of letters from sorcery, and was acquitted.

log.rubric: THE TRIBUNAL · THE SECOND INQUISITION
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — he wins the first two inquisitions; exact years not established in sources in hand
log.situation: They have learned. This time the charge quotes your own circulated work back at you, in context, with the difficult passage on the board. There is no procedural escape from a quotation you actually wrote.

options.label: Defend the passage as written
options.detail: Stand on the text. Explain what it means and refuse to disown it.

options.label: Let your patron end it
options.detail: Political protection instead of argument. Fast, humiliating, and it spends real capital.

options.label: Disown the passage
options.detail: Sacrifice one formulation to save the whole. Survivable. Corrosive.

log.outcomeText: You take the panel through the passage until the difficulty dissolves into the argument it belongs to. Acquitted, and two of the panel ask for copies afterward.

chronicle.orig: At the second tribunal he defended the disputed passage until his judges asked for copies of it.
chronicle.current: At the second tribunal he defended the disputed passage until his judges asked for copies of it.

log.rubric: THE TRIBUNAL · THE THIRD INQUISITION
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — he loses the third, datable to c. 1427; five years of wandering exile follow, death 1432
log.situation: The third is different. The panel is chosen, not assembled; the charge is broad enough to cover a life; and the question underneath every question is simply whether a man may build a science the state has not authorized. This is the one the record says he loses. The record was not written by you.

plate.caption: Hilye-i Şerif — calligraphic description of the Prophet, Ottoman (Wikimedia Commons)

options.label: Hold firm and refuse to bend
options.detail: The historically attested answer. It costs everything and concedes nothing.

options.label: Recant
options.detail: Say the words. Keep the life, the post, and nothing else.

options.label: Give them a name
options.detail: They will settle for a bigger heretic than you. Qāsim is already suspect.

options.label: Do not appear
options.detail: Take the road before the verdict. Condemned in absentia; free, and finished here.

log.outcomeText: They condemn. The sentence is not death — it is worse arranged than that: removal, disgrace, and the road.

chronicle.orig: He refused to bend, and the third tribunal condemned him.
chronicle.current: He refused to bend, and the third tribunal condemned him.

log.rubric: THE EASTERN GATE · A CHECKPOINT WITH YOUR NAME AT IT
log.source: The sīmiyā signature moment (VN PROPOSAL: escape by misdirection); the five-year exile itself is ATTESTED
log.situation: The sentence entitles you to leave; a clerk’s addendum entitles the governor to everything you carry. At the eastern gate the soldiers have a list, and your baggage — books, tables, the years of paper — is exactly what the list is for. The exile may pass. The archive may not.

options.label: Let them seize the wrong chest
options.detail: Sīmiyā at last: a decoy chest, a staged reluctance, and every eye drawn where you want it.

options.label: Pay what the soldiers ask
options.detail: Coin instead of craft. It empties the purse that was meant to last five years.

options.label: Let them take the chests
options.detail: The work is in other hands or it is nowhere. Walk out with a staff and a cloak.

log.outcomeText: Expensive, effective, unremarkable. The books pass as “personal effects.” Poverty arrives a year early.

chronicle.orig: He bought his archive through the eastern gate, and began his exile poorer than the sentence required.
chronicle.current: He bought his archive through the eastern gate, and began his exile poorer than the sentence required.

log.rubric: THE ROAD · WHAT IS LEFT
log.source: BIOGRAPHY — five years of wandering exile after the third inquisition; death 1432, impoverished, in legal limbo
log.situation: However the tribunals fell out, the years after them are the ones that decide what this life was. There is a road, a diminishing amount of money, and a body of work that is either travelling without you or sitting in a box. What you do with the last of it is the last decision you get.

plate.caption: Teardrop cosmological diagram — Shams al-Maʿārif, p. 256 (Wikimedia Commons)

options.label: Teach wherever they let you stop
options.detail: Turn exile into transmission. No security, maximum spread.

options.label: Finish the work
options.detail: Complete the system, alone, whether or not anyone is left to read it.

options.label: Petition, negotiate, rebuild
options.detail: Spend the last years trying to get the standing back. It sometimes works.

options.label: Entrust everything to the circle and stop
options.detail: Hand it over. Let the movement be the movement; be an old man.

log.outcomeText: You teach where you can. It is thinner than a school and more durable than a book.

chronicle.orig: He spent his last years teaching on the road, thinly and durably.
chronicle.current: He spent his last years teaching on the road, thinly and durably.
